title: Surface Tension

notes.heading: 1. Surface Tension, Surface Energy & Droplet Coalescence
notes.proseLatex: Surface tension $S = F/\ell$ ($\text{N/m}$) equals isothermal surface energy per unit free area $W/\Delta A$ ($\text{J/m}^2$, dimension $[MT^{-2}]$). A liquid DROP in air has ONE free surface ($\Delta A = 4\pi R^2$), whereas a SOAP FILM or SOAP BUBBLE in air has TWO free air-liquid interfaces ($\Delta A = 2\times 4\pi R^2 = 8\pi R^2$). When $n$ identical droplets of radius $r$ coalesce into one big drop of radius $R$, volume conservation gives $R = n^{1/3}r$ and surface area shrinks, RELEASING heat.

keyFormulas.label: Drop vs Soap-Bubble Work & Coalescence Energy
keyFormulas.latex: $W_{\text{drop}} = 4\pi R^2 S,\quad W_{\text{soap bubble}} = 8\pi R^2 S,\quad R = n^{1/3}r,\quad \Delta U_{\text{rel}} = 4\pi R^2 S(n^{1/3} - 1)$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Count 1 vs 2 free surfaces and compute energy absorbed on splitting or released on merging.

examples.problemLatex: Work required to split a water drop of radius $R$ into $64$ identical droplets (surface tension $S$)?
stepsLatex: Volume conservation: $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 64\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies r = R/4$.
$W = S(A_f - A_i) = S\bigl[64\cdot 4\pi(R/4)^2 - 4\pi R^2\bigr] = S(16\pi R^2 - 4\pi R^2) = 12\pi R^2 S$.

notes.heading: 2. Young-Laplace Excess Pressure & Communicating Soap Bubbles
notes.proseLatex: The concave side of any curved meniscus sits at higher pressure than the convex side. Excess pressure inside a liquid drop (or an air bubble submerged INSIDE water — 1 interface!) is $\Delta P = \frac{2S}{R}$, whereas inside a soap bubble in air (2 interfaces!) it doubles to $\Delta P = \frac{4S}{R}$. Since $\Delta P \propto 1/R$, when a small soap bubble and a large soap bubble are connected by a tube, air flows from the SMALLER bubble into the LARGER bubble!

keyFormulas.label: Laplace Excess Pressure (Drop / Air Bubble vs Soap Bubble)
keyFormulas.latex: $\Delta P_{\text{drop or underwater bubble}} = \frac{2S}{R},\qquad \Delta P_{\text{soap bubble in air}} = \frac{4S}{R}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Distinguish 2S/R (1 interface) from 4S/R (2 interfaces) and bubble coalescence radius.

notes.heading: 3. Angle of Contact, Jurin's Capillary Law & Tube of Insufficient Length
notes.proseLatex: Wetting liquids ($\theta < 90^\circ$, e.g., pure water on clean glass $\theta \approx 0^\circ$) form a concave meniscus and RISE in a capillary tube, while non-wetting liquids ($\theta > 90^\circ$, e.g., mercury on glass $\theta \approx 135^\circ$) form a convex meniscus and DEPRESS. Jurin's formula gives $h = \frac{2S\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$. If the capillary tube protrudes less than $h$ above the bath, water does NOT overflow as a fountain — instead the meniscus flattens ($R_m$ increases) so $h' R_m = h R_{m,0} = \text{const}$.

keyFormulas.label: Jurin's Capillary Rise Formula
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Predict capillary rise/depression and meniscus adjustment in short tubes.

examples.problemLatex: Water rises to $6\text{ cm}$ in a vertical glass capillary. If a tube of half the radius is used, how high does water rise?
stepsLatex: By Jurin's law $h \propto 1/r$ for the same liquid-solid pair and gravity.

wbjeebTraps: An AIR bubble INSIDE water has only ONE air-water interface ($\Delta P = 2S/R$), whereas a SOAP bubble in air has TWO ($\Delta P = 4S/R$).
Smaller bubble has HIGHER internal pressure ($\Delta P \propto 1/R$): connecting a small and a large soap bubble makes the small one shrink and the large one grow!
Water NEVER overflows out of a capillary of insufficient length — the meniscus curvature simply adjusts.
